reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A RASopathy caused by germline activating variants in HRAS, distinguishing it from Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes at the molecular level
The face is coarse with full lips, a wide mouth, epicanthic folds and low-set ears, becoming more marked with age
Deep palmar and plantar creases with soft, loose skin and papillomata around the nose and mouth are characteristic cutaneous clues
There is a substantial risk of both benign and malignant tumours, notably rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma and bladder carcinoma, mandating structured surveillance
Failure to thrive with severe feeding difficulty often necessitating tube feeding is usual in infancy despite a large birth weight
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia (particularly atrial tachycardia) and pulmonary stenosis are important cardiac features
Almost all cases are de novo and follow autosomal dominant inheritance
reference.pathophysiology: Costello syndrome is caused by germline activating variants in HRAS, a small GTPase that is a central switch of the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway controlling cell growth, differentiation and survival. Pathogenic variants lock HRAS in an active, GTP-bound state, driving constitutive downstream signalling. This sustained activation not only disturbs craniofacial, cardiac and connective-tissue development but also promotes cellular proliferation, explaining the characteristic phenotype and the notably elevated predisposition to embryonal tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Mucopolysaccharidoses and other storage disorders with coarse features
additionalInvestigations: Targeted HRAS sequencing, or RASopathy gene-panel testing
Echocardiography and electrocardiography for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, pulmonary stenosis and arrhythmia
Tumour surveillance including abdominal and pelvic ultrasound and urinalysis for haematuria per established protocols
Growth and nutritional assessment with feeding evaluation
Brain and spine imaging for Chiari I malformation and syringomyelia when clinically indicated
Endocrine assessment for growth hormone deficiency and hypoglycaemia
redFlags: New mass, unexplained pain or haematuria prompting urgent tumour evaluation
Palpitations or signs of atrial tachyarrhythmia and cardiomyopathy
Failure to thrive and dehydration from severe feeding difficulty
Neurological signs suggesting Chiari malformation or syringomyelia
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced primarily by cardiac complications, especially cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, and by malignancy; structured tumour surveillance improves early detection. Intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate, and affected individuals often have a sociable, engaging personality.
pitfalls: Failing to institute tumour surveillance given the high embryonal cancer risk
Misclassifying it as Noonan or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, altering cancer risk counselling
Overlooking atrial tachyarrhythmia that may be intermittent
Attributing infantile feeding failure to reflux alone and delaying tube feeding
